item.title: Permit L Freiburg: validity and extension
item.description: The short-term L permit allows foreigners to work in Switzerland for up to 1 year. Learn about extension rules, employer constraints, and how to switch to B and C permits.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The L permit allows you to work in Switzerland for a maximum of 1 year - Extension is possible but depends on federal criteria and job availability - The permit is specifically tied to the employer and professional sector
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term permit for foreign workers - Maximum duration: 1 year - Scope: Canton of Fribourg (federal SEM system) - Managed by: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level - Main restriction: Tied to the specific employer indicated in the permit
The short-term L permit is the regulatory tool through which Switzerland authorizes foreign workers to engage in dependent professional activities within the national territory. Managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level, the L permit applies identically across all Swiss cantons, including the Canton of Fribourg, without additional authorizations from the cantonal administration beyond those stipulated by federal regulations.
### Maximum duration of the L permit
According to federal regulations, the L permit has a maximum validity of 1 year. This means that the foreign worker can reside and work in Switzerland for a period not exceeding 12 months from the date of issuance. Unlike residence (B) or settlement (C) permits, the L permit does not offer long-term stay and requires an explicit extension if the employment relationship continues beyond the initial term.
The L permit is specifically named after the employer: this means that the worker cannot change jobs without a formal modification to the permit itself. If the employment relationship ends before the expiration date, the permit automatically lapses, and the worker must leave the national territory or apply for a new permit for a new job position. This restriction reflects the objective of Swiss migration policy to anchor the permit to the actual economic need of the employer.
The procedure for obtaining the L permit begins before the foreigner's arrival in Switzerland. The employer submits the application to the competent cantonal office in Fribourg, attaching the employment contract, the candidate's identity documents, and sometimes professional qualification certificates. Once authorized, the permit allows entry and commencement of work activities according to the modalities specified in the document. ### Conditions of extension and constraints with the employer
The extension of the L permit is not automatic. When the permit is about to expire within 12 months of initial validity, the employer must submit a new application for renewal to the competent cantonal office. The extension is granted on the condition that the economic and working conditions justifying the initial authorisation still exist. In particular, the cantonal office verifies that the employment relationship continues to be active and that there are no significant changes in the contractual conditions.
If the employer does not submit the request for an extension before the expiry date, the permit automatically ceases and the worker cannot continue to work as a wage earner in Switzerland. There are no transition periods or tacit extensions: the deadline is peremptory and binding.
An important aspect concerns the constraint on the specific employer. While the permit is valid, the worker cannot change employer autonomously. If the worker wishes to move to a different job, the new employer must submit a new application for an L permit to the cantonal office. This means that the change of employment is not immediate: the permit must be formally modified by the administration. In the meantime, the worker cannot start the new work activity.

item.title: Legumes with meat textures: ETH Zurich research
item.description: ETH researchers transform peas, beans and lentils into products with a fibrous meat-like structure, reducing food waste.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ETH Zurich researchers transform legumes into fibrous structure similar to meat. - The method reduces food waste while preserving nutritional value. - Simple process: soaking, pureeing, heating, freezing the mass. - Applicable also in domestic kitchens; recipes developed by professional chefs.
## Key facts - **What**: Transformation of legumes (peas, beans, lentils) into products with fibrous texture - Who: Researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH), coordinated by Patrick Rühs - Where: ETH Zurich laboratories - How: Soaking legumes → pureeing → heating → freezing to create oriented lamellae - Why: Reduce food waste in industrial processes and preserve nutritional value - Legumes: Peas, beans and lentils (96% of world production) - When: Study published in the specialized journal "NJP Science of Food" - Application: Simple method replicable also in domestic kitchens
The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich has developed an innovative process to transform common legumes — peas, beans and lentils — into products with a fibrous consistency comparable to that of meat. The announcement comes directly from the Zurich researchers, who primarily aim to reduce food waste in the food production sector.
In contemporary industrial production, raw materials are frequently decomposed into their essential components: proteins, starch and fats are separated and then recombined to create new products. During this process, a significant portion of the raw material is not utilized, generating considerable losses. The new method developed at ETH allows legumes to be transformed without losses into a food with an oriented and fibrous structure, maintaining the original nutritional value intact.
"A fibrous structure provides, during chewing, a sensation that many people appreciate in meat and fish," explains Professor Patrick Rühs in an official statement from the institution. "In meat or fish, this fibrous structure is the result of the arrangement of muscle fibers," adds the researcher, highlighting how the new process artificially reproduces the same effect.
### The transformation process
The methodology is surprisingly straightforward. The researchers initially soaked the legumes in water, then reduced them to a puree. Subsequently, this puree is heated until it acquires a gelatinous appearance. The crucial step is the freezing of the mass: during this stage, oriented lamellar structures are formed in the same direction. Once thawed, the product maintains this fibrous configuration stably.
Tests involved various varieties of beans, peas and lentils. The researchers observed variations in the final consistencies depending on the variety and water content. For example, red lentils produced a more compact structure compared to soybeans. "Our process works with a wide range of legumes, which represent 96% of world production," emphasizes Patrick Rühs.
### Simplicity of application and development prospects
A particularly relevant aspect of the new method is its accessibility: "The new method is so simple that anyone can apply it without problems in their own kitchen," says doctoral student Andrea Bach, directly involved in the research. This feature distinguishes it from complex industrial processes and makes it potentially usable by domestic consumers.
The ETH study was published in the specialized journal "NJP Science of Food," providing a solid scientific basis for the results. As a continuation of the project, the researchers intend to examine more closely how to control and modulate the different final consistencies of the product. The development of concrete recipes has been entrusted to professional chefs, indicating an interest in the practical culinary application of the method. ### Impact on sustainability and the Swiss food industry
The ETH research fits into an international context of growing attention to reducing food waste. According to UST (Federal Statistical Office) data, the Swiss food industry generates significant losses during industrial processing. This new method represents a concrete step towards optimizing production processes while simultaneously preserving the nutritional profile of foods.
The Swiss food industry, characterized by high quality standards, could directly benefit from this innovation. Legumes are relatively inexpensive raw materials, and transforming them into products with sensory properties comparable to meat could open interesting market segments, both for domestic consumption and export. Although Switzerland is not a major legume producer, it imports significant quantities from various regions of the world, particularly Europe and North Africa.
### Implications for the cost of living and legume prices
In the current context of attention to the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), the economic accessibility of legumes is a relevant factor. Legumes are low-cost plant proteins compared to meat, and improvements in processing could further reduce consumer prices. This is particularly significant for those living in cantons with higher costs of living, such as Zurich and Basel-City.
The VAT on food in Switzerland is set at 2.5% for foodstuffs, the lowest among standard rates. If legumes processed according to the new method enter the market as a shelf product, they will benefit from the same favorable taxation, maintaining competitive prices for consumers. Additionally, by reducing waste in the industrial production phase, producers could pass on part of these savings to Swiss consumers.
### Transition to mindful diets
The global trend towards plant-based diets is also growing in Switzerland. Legumes, rich in proteins and fibers, are increasingly considered valid alternatives to animal proteins. The new ETH process does not require complex chemical additives and works with 100% of the raw material, making it particularly attractive from a sustainability perspective.
Sensory perception remains a crucial factor: many consumers still choose meat because they appreciate the characteristic fibrous texture. If processed legumes could replicate this chewing sensation, they could win over a segment of consumers previously reluctant to plant proteins. In the long term, innovations of this type contribute to stabilizing the prices of plant proteins in the Swiss market, reducing dependence on meat imports and promoting a more mindful food transition.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to replicate the method at home
For those who wish to experiment with the new process in their home kitchen, the procedure is accessible and does not require specialized equipment. Here are the essential steps to obtain legumes with a fibrous consistency.
**Step 1 - Preparation**: Take dry legumes (red lentils, common beans, dried peas) and soak them in cold water for at least 8-12 hours. This step is crucial to soften the legumes and facilitate the subsequent transformation.
Step 2 - Reduction to puree: After soaking, drain the legumes and reduce them to a puree using a blender or food processor. The final consistency should be homogeneous, similar to a thick mashed potato compound.
Step 3 - Gelatinous heating: Transfer the puree to a pot and heat it over moderate heat, stirring continuously. This phase serves to evaporate some of the water and give the mass a gelatinous appearance. The time required depends on the amount and initial water content, but generally 15-20 minutes are sufficient.
Step 4 - Freezing: Once the desired consistency is reached, transfer the mass to a container suitable for freezing (tray or jar) and place in the freezer for at least 24 hours. During this phase, the lamellar structures that will give the final fibrous texture are formed.
Step 5 - Thawing and use: Remove the product from the freezer and let it thaw at room temperature or in the refrigerator. Once thawed, it will retain the oriented fibrous structure. The product can be used as a base for vegetable meatballs, burgers, legume ragù, or other dishes that require a hearty texture.
### Choosing the most suitable legumes
Not all legumes will produce the same consistency. According to ETH research data, red lentils generate a more compact texture, while other legumes such as soybeans produce slightly more crumbly structures. It is recommended to start with red lentils or red beans, both easily available in Swiss grocery stores and specialized organic markets.
### Obtaining Swiss legumes and employment in the sector
Although Switzerland is not among the world's leading legume producers, several cantons (particularly Vaud, Fribourg, and Geneva) cultivate modest amounts of organic legumes. To support local production and reduce the carbon footprint, it is advisable to check with local farmers' markets, cantonal agricultural cooperatives, and certified organic product stores for the availability of legumes grown in Switzerland. The development of recipes is entrusted to professionals in the culinary sector, highlighting how food innovation generates qualified employment in Switzerland.
### Next steps and practical resource
ETH research continues to develop new formulations and refine the control of consistencies. To understand how conscious food choices influence your monthly budget and what your potential savings are, [consult our calculator to analyze your economic situation](nav:calculator). Small daily choices — such as the use of plant proteins — can significantly impact your cost of living.

item.title: L Fribourg permit: duration and renewal
item.description: L Freiburg permit: valid for up to 1 year, renewal and transition to B and C permits. Procedures, documents and employer constraints.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The L permit is valid for up to 1 year and is intended for temporary work in Switzerland - It is renewable upon joint request with the employer, under the same conditions - From the L permit you pass to B (residence, 5 years) and then to C (residence, 10 years)
## Key Facts - **What**: Residence permit and temporary work for foreigners in Switzerland - Duration: Up to 1 year (not automatically renewable; renewal on request) - Where: Canton of Fribourg (federal SEM regulations for all cantons) - Who: Secrétariat d'État aux migrations (SEM) — federal competence; cantonal administration by cantonal procedure - Local authority: Office of Employment and Migration of the Canton of Fribourg
### What is the L permit and how does it work
The short-term L permit is the instrument through which Switzerland regulates the temporary entry of foreign workers. It is valid for a maximum of 12 months and allows you to live and work in the country during this period. Unlike other permits (B for residence, C for domicile), the L permit does not offer long-term stability, but is an ideal solution for temporary, seasonal or project-specific assignments.
In the canton of Fribourg, as in all other Swiss cantons, the L permit is subject to the federal regulation of the Secrétariat d'État aux migrations. There are no specific cantonal variants that differentiate the conditions in Fribourg from other cantons: the rules on duration, renewal and contractual obligations remain uniform at the national level. The cantonal administrative procedure, however, is handled by the office of the canton of Fribourg responsible for employment and immigration.
### Who can get it and employer constraints
The L permit is subject to the submission of a genuine job offer. The Swiss employer (or the Swiss branch of a foreign company) must prove that it cannot find a resource available on the domestic market and that the position is actually necessary. This check is carried out by the competent authorities when submitting the application.
The employer remains the real "anchor" of the permit: the L permit is nominative, i.e. in the name of a specific company, and the worker cannot change employer without the re-registration procedure and new approval by the SEM and the canton. This is a fundamental constraint that distinguishes the L permit from the simple authorization to reside. It means that the permit is linked to the permanence in the same workplace and that any change requires timely notification to the authorities. ### Renewal of the L permit and conditions for extension
An L permit can be renewed, but renewal is not automatic. The procedure requires a new joint application by the employer and the foreigner to the Fribourg cantonal administration, preferably submitted 60-90 days before expiry. Renewal is possible if the initial conditions are still met: the employer confirms the employment need, the employment is real and continues, and there are no legal impediments such as no criminal record, tax regularity, and timely payment of social contributions (AHV/IV, unemployment insurance, health insurance).
The duration of each renewal period is still up to 1 year. There is no theoretical limit to the number of consecutive renewals, as long as the conditions remain met. However, the Swiss permit system is designed to incentivize temporariness: if the employment becomes structural and permanent, it is more convenient for everyone (employer, employee, cantonal authority) to transition to a B (residence) permit, which offers a validity of 5 years and less administrative bureaucracy.
### Transition from L to B: when and how
After the first year of the L permit (or after one or more consecutive renewals), the transition to the B permit is the natural step. The B permit is valid for 5 years and can be renewed indefinitely, representing significantly greater stability. To access the B permit, there is no need to change cantons: the canton of Fribourg remains the competent party. The administrative procedure is handled by the Fribourg office, which automatically assesses the possibility of transition once the first L permit has expired and if the requirements are met.
Minimum requirements for the transition to B include: documented actual employment for at least 1 year (demonstrable with payslips, renewed contracts); absence of pending sanctions or expulsion measures; regular and full payment of social contributions; ability to economic self-sufficiency, demonstrated by the net income that allows you to live without cantonal public support.
### Difference Between B and C Permit
The C permit (domicile) represents the final step in the progression. It is generally available after 10 years of continuous legal residence (or 5 years for citizens of the European Union or the European Economic Area), and offers almost absolute stability. Unlike the B permit, the C permit allows for wider job mobility: it is possible to change employer and sector with fewer administrative constraints and without the need for a new authorization for each change.
In addition, the C permit is a prerequisite for accessing ordinary Swiss naturalization, which then requires the C permit plus 10 years of actual residence, together with the requirements established by the canton and municipality of residence.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### Step-by-step: how to renew your L permit in Freiburg
The renewal procedure is managed by the Fribourg cantonal administration. Here are the operational steps:
Step 1 — Coordination with the employer (60-90 days before expiration): The employer and the employee must agree on the willingness to renew. It is essential that the employer confirms in writing the stable employment and the need to continue employment beyond the expiration date of the current permit.
Step 2 — Collection of documentation: the employer prepares a reasoned declaration (explaining the reasons for continuing), the renewed or extended employment contract, the worker's last 3 pay slips, a copy of the company's tax return for the last 2 financial years, and (if the employee has resided in Switzerland for more than 2 years) a certificate of good conduct.
Step 3 — Submission of the application: joint application (employer + employee, preferably with both signatures certified) to the competent office in the canton of Fribourg (usually the employment or migration desk). Check whether the canton accepts digital applications via the SEM platform or whether it requires paper documentation.
Step 4 — Verification and timing: The canton of Fribourg takes an average of 4-8 weeks to evaluate the application. It is not mandatory for the permit to be renewed BEFORE it expires (the employee can take advantage of a short tolérance during the verification procedure), but it is advisable to submit the application in time to avoid interruptions.
Step 5 — Issuance and Communication: Once approved, the positive decision is notified to both the employer and the employee. The renewed permit is valid for an additional 12 months from the date of approval.
### Documents required for renewal
- Valid passport and photocopy of personal page - Renewed or extended employment contract (with signature of both parties) - Last 3 pay slips (payslip) - Company tax return (last 2 tax years) - Certificate of good conduct (if resident for more than 2 years) - Statement of account from the provident fund (AHV/IV) to check the regularity of contributions
### When it is convenient to switch from permission L to B
If the renewal of the L permit becomes recurrent (more than 2 consecutive renewals, i.e. more than 3 years of stay), it is advisable to consider switching to B. Concrete advantages: less bureaucracy (renewal every 5 years instead of every year); expanded labor mobility (possibility of changing employer with a simplified procedure); recognition of stable and long-term residence, with tax and social security benefits.
Conversely, if the occupation is actually temporary (maximum 2-3 years), the L permit remains the most pragmatic choice: less administrative effort, and no obligation to transition to B.
### Support and practical tools
Further information on cantonal specific procedures and application forms can be found on the official website of the administration of the canton of Fribourg (www.fr.ch, Employment and Migration section).
To check the regularity of the payments of social contributions (AHV/IV) and to calculate the actual amounts withheld from the payroll, the [calcolatore di stipendio e contributi](nav:calculator) is available, which also allows you to estimate the applicable tax deductions.

item.title: Switzerland's taxis: world's most expensive
item.description: A 10km ride in Lucerne costs 58.89 francs, making the Swiss city the most expensive in the world for taxis.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Lucerne has the most expensive taxis in the world - A 10 km ride costs 58.89 francs - Waiting fees increase the price
## Key facts - **What**: Analysis of taxi fares - When: Summer 2024 - Where: Lucerne, Switzerland - Who: British insurance company Zego - Amount: 58.89 francs for 10 km
Switzerland remains the country with the most expensive taxis in the world, despite Iceland overtaking Switzerland as the most expensive country in the world. This is highlighted by an analysis from the British insurance company Zego, which examined locations where taxi prices were highest this summer. The analysis, conducted across over 1,000 cities worldwide, aimed to show what tourists can expect when traveling from the airport to the city center. The result: five of the ten cities with the highest taxi costs are in Switzerland, with Lucerne at the top. The Principality of Liechtenstein also features in the ranking.
### High Fares In Lucerne, a ten-kilometer ride with a ten-minute waiting fee costs 58.89 francs. Converted, this is ten cents more than Palm Springs, the California desert city known as a holiday destination for Hollywood stars like Leonardo Di Caprio. The authors of the price comparison emphasize the high average starting price in Lucerne, at 6.63 francs. In Zurich, it is even higher, while in Lausanne and Basel, it is only slightly lower. In Swiss cities, waiting costs are particularly high.
### Tips for Travelers Zego's director, Sten Saar, states: 'What many people are not aware of is that traffic can significantly increase the cost of a taxi ride, even if the distance remains the same. Airports are often located on the outskirts of the city, so arriving during peak hours or periods of high demand can significantly increase the final price due to waiting fees and slower traffic.' For Saar, prices like those in Zurich are no surprise. And he observes enthusiastically: 'With some of the most expensive and exclusive boutiques in the world, and ski resorts just a few kilometers away, it's no wonder Zurich is among the cities with the highest taxi fares globally.'
His advice applies to all cities: check local fares, compare public transport and airport transfers, or, if available, use fixed-price services. This way, spending a few minutes planning before arrival could save much more than looking for a cheaper flight. ### Implications for Residents and Tourists High taxi fares in Switzerland, and particularly in Lucerne, have significant implications for both residents and tourists. For residents, these fares can influence everyday transportation decisions, prompting many to opt for public transportation or car-sharing solutions. For tourists, planning becomes crucial to avoid unexpected costs. Knowledge of local fares and the ability to use fixed-price services can make all the difference.
### Comparison with Other Swiss Cities Lucerne is not the only Swiss city with high fares. Zurich, Lausanne and Basel have particularly high waiting fares, making taxi rides expensive even for short distances. This comparison highlights how Switzerland is unique in the world, with fares that even exceed those of luxurious cities such as Palm Springs.
### Strategies to Save Money For residents and tourists, there are several strategies to save money on taxi costs. Using public transportation, which is efficient and well-connected in Switzerland, can be a cost-effective solution. Additionally, comparing the fares of different taxi services and opting for those that offer fixed prices can help avoid surprises. Planning ahead and knowing local fares are crucial for better managing transportation costs.

item.title: Wind energy: Federal hearing for new plants
item.description: On 1 September, the ARE is launching the consultation of the cantons and the public on adapting the wind energy concept and strengthening planning security.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ARE hearing for adaptation of the wind energy concept from 1 September 2026 - Procedure open to cantons and public participation nationwide - Objective: to strengthen planning and increase the construction of wind farms - Required to align with new legal provisions and regulatory bases
## Key Facts - **What**: Adaptation of Switzerland's Wind Energy Concept - When: 1 September 2026 (start date of the hearing) - Where: Switzerland (federal procedure involving cantons) - Who: Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE) - Type of procedure: Hearing of the cantons + public participation - Purpose: To adapt the Conception to new legal provisions and new regulatory bases - Expected result: Strengthen planning security for authorities and managers; increase the probability of new wind farms being built
On 1 September 2026, the Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE) initiated the hearing of the cantons and public participation to adapt Switzerland's Wind Energy Concept. The procedure is necessary to incorporate the new legal provisions and new foundations that have characterized recent regulatory developments in the energy sector. The adaptation is not just a technical revision: it aims to strengthen the security of spatial planning for local authorities and wind project managers, and at the same time to concretely increase the chances of new wind farms being built on Swiss territory.
### What is the Wind Energy Conception
The Wind Energy Concept is a federal planning instrument that defines the principles and criteria for the establishment of wind farms on Swiss territory. It provides the framework for cantons, municipalities and project promoters to identify suitable areas for the construction of wind turbines, balancing energy needs, landscape protection and environmental considerations. This instrument reflects the federal competence in spatial planning and national energy strategy, while remaining subject to coordination with specific cantonal policies. The periodic adaptation of the Concept ensures that the instrument remains consistent with the evolution of energy and spatial legislation. ### Why Adjustment Is Necessary
The adaptation of the Wind Energy Concept stems from the need to align the instrument with the new legal provisions recently introduced in the Swiss regulatory framework. The ARE communication points out that the change was made necessary by the change in the legal bases governing wind energy. Although the source does not specify the individual amended laws, it is clear that the federal legislator considered it essential to update the procedural and substantive framework to ensure regulatory consistency.
The hearing procedure is the lever through which the federal government involves local institutions and civil society in the decision-making process. The cantons, which have significant autonomy in spatial planning, will be able to provide feedback on the adaptation based on their specific energy and spatial needs. Public participation, simultaneous with the cantonal hearing, allows citizens, interested bodies and project managers to express opinions and observations that will be evaluated by the ARE before the final version of the Conception.
### Implications for cantonal planning
Enhanced planning security means that authorities and promoters will have a clearer and more predictable tool when defining where to build wind farms. Less regulatory ambiguity translates into faster permitting times, reduced legal risks and increased investor confidence in the domestic wind sector. On the other hand, the objective of increasing the likelihood of new wind farms being built signals that the ARE has recognised the need to simplify or facilitate the deployment of wind turbines, probably in response to the national energy strategy that aims to increase the share of renewable energy in electricity generation. The cantons participating in the hearing will have the opportunity to negotiate the boundaries and criteria of the Conception to adapt them to the local territory, avoiding future conflicts between federal planning and cantonal decisions.

Public participation is open to anyone wishing to submit an opinion on the adaptation of the Wind Energy Concept. This includes individual citizens, environmental associations, local authorities, companies, industry organisations and any other stakeholders interested in wind planning in Switzerland. The consultation is a real opportunity to influence the federal decision-making process and to raise concerns, suggestions or support for the adaptation of the planning tool.
To participate, you must follow the procedures indicated by the ARE in the official documentation of the public consultation. Although the source does not specify the exact procedural details (forms, email address, digital platforms, precise deadlines), you can contact the Federal Office for Spatial Development directly to obtain the necessary information and access the participation tools made available. The ARE is the body responsible for the procedure and provides all the instructions for submitting comments and comments.
### Deadlines and next steps
The ARE communication announces that the hearing was launched on 1 September 2026, but does not specify the closing date of the consultation. It is prudent to contact the Federal Office for Spatial Development in good time to find out the deadline for submitting your opinions, in order not to miss the opportunity to participate. Once the hearing and public comments phase has been concluded, the ARE will analyse the feedback received and proceed with the update of the Wind Energy Concept. The specific timeline for the final approval of the amended version was not communicated in the source, but will follow the federal standard administrative processes that involve review, interdepartmental coordination and possibly further consultations.
The adaptation of the Wind Energy Concept is an important element of Swiss energy policy. Participating in the consultation allows citizens, local authorities and operators to influence a decision-making process that will have a concrete impact on the growth of wind farms over the next decade. To follow the progress of the procedure and access the official consultation documents, please contact the Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE) directly through official federal channels.

item.title: Swiss mobile telephony: Comcom excludes new providers
item.description: The Swiss Federal Communications Commission states: Economic and regulatory barriers make it virtually impossible for new competitors to enter the mobile phone market.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Comcom excludes new entrants: insurmountable economic and regulatory hurdles - Minimum cost: CHF 500 million to build your own network - Three current operators (Swisscom, Salt, Sunrise) will remain dominant - By 2033: Starlink should also build terrestrial networks in Switzerland
## Key Facts - **What**: Comcom declares it impossible for new competitors to enter mobile telephony - When: Statements by President Martin Bürki on Tuesday on the sidelines of the press conference - Where: Switzerland, national mobile market - Who: Federal Communications Commission (Comcom); current providers: Swisscom, Salt, Sunrise - Minimum amount: CHF 500 million to build own network - Deadline: 2033 to reach coverage of 50% of the population
The Swiss Federal Communications Commission (Comcom) does not foresee the entry of new players into the mobile phone market. President Martin Bürki confirmed on Tuesday, on the sidelines of a press conference in Bern in talks with the AWP news agency, that the economic and regulatory obstacles are simply too high for any competitor.
The construction of its own mobile network would cost, according to a rough estimate, at least half a billion Swiss francs. To this figure must be added the costs of setting up a sales and management organization in Switzerland. The difficulties do not end there: the new entrant would have to meet the minimum coverage requirement of 50% of the population.
### Regulatory and geographical walls that stop new entrants
Finding suitable spaces to install antennas is a second almost insurmountable obstacle. In Swiss cities, it is already very difficult to locate new antenna sites. In addition, there are restrictions imposed by the Federal Radiation Protection Regulation (NISV), which further limit the possible placement of infrastructure.
Comcom member Jean Christophe Schwaab stressed during the press conference that the commission would check very carefully whether a new entrant would be able to operate a mobile network covering half of the population by 2033. "A new entrant has to prove that it is technically and financially capable of doing this," he said.
This obligation would also apply to satellite operators such as Elon Musk's Starlink: they would also have to build their own terrestrial network, as satellite-only coverage does not meet Swiss requirements. According to Bürki, satellite-only coverage would only affect limited areas and cause interference in border regions. The auctioned frequencies are also not intended for the use of satellite communication.
As a result, it is very unlikely that a fourth bidder will appear at the next frequency auction in addition to the current operators Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise. ## How Comcom balances competition between three operators
Comcom, however, does not want a completely closed market. President Bürki said he wanted to maintain "three strong players in the market, which ultimately guarantee a good customer experience." The goal is to maintain functional competition between the three incumbents, avoiding scenarios in which one is the clear winner and one is the clear loser.
To achieve this balance, Comcom has introduced bidding constraints in the upcoming mobile frequency auction. According to Bürki, "we have tried to eliminate this risk."
### Spectrum limits: the new regulatory strategy
Bidding restrictions have been significantly tightened compared to the past. A single operator can purchase a maximum of 230 megahertz (MHz) of spectrum, which corresponds to around 43% of all available frequencies. In the previous auction in 2012, the upper limit was 270 MHz, or 50% of the total spectrum.
In addition to the general limit, Comcom has introduced specific restrictions for each frequency band, a measure that was absent from the 2012 auction:
- **Low band (800–900 MHz)**: a single bidder can be awarded a maximum of 38% of the available frequencies - Mid-band (1800–2100 MHz): the upper limit is set at two-thirds of the spectrum of that band - High-band (2600 MHz FDD): the limit rises to 71% of the available frequencies
These constraints aim to distribute the spectrum in a more balanced way among the three operators, preventing one of them from accumulating excessive market power. The regulatory model reflects a conscious choice by Comcom: to accept a stable oligopoly of three strong operators rather than risk a competitive war that could damage the national infrastructure.
### Regulatory stability versus new competition
The combination of structural economic barriers (the CHF 500 million for the initial infrastructure) and regulatory constraints makes the Swiss mobile market de facto closed to new entrants. Consumers will continue to choose between Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise, with competition regulated by Comcom rather than organic market forces. This approach sacrifices market openness in favour of infrastructure stability and the guarantee of widespread territorial coverage.

The closure of the market to new competitors has direct implications for Swiss residents and employees. On the one hand, they will not see the emergence of alternative operators that could offer more aggressive tariffs or innovative services. On the other hand, Comcom aims to prevent excessive power concentrations that would marginalize some operators, thus ensuring a choice between three stable and reliable providers.
Those who want to switch mobile providers in the coming years will choose between Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise, based on price, geographical coverage, mobile internet speed and quality of customer service. No new global competitors will emerge to disturb this balance in the medium term.
### Deadline 2033: Comcom's benchmark
The deadline by 2033 to reach 50% population coverage is a key milestone in Comcom's strategy. This is the benchmark that the committee will use to assess whether a hypothetical new entrant can legally operate in Switzerland. So far, no entity has expressed any intention to present itself as a new candidate for the next frequency auctions.
### How to monitor Comcom's decisions
If you wish to follow the development of the Swiss mobile market, you can consult Comcom's public documents on the official federal website. Spectrum auctions are public procedures: the results, winners and frequencies awarded are officially announced. Comcom will continue to monitor whether the three operators are meeting their territorial coverage and infrastructure investment commitments. Consumers who find mobile phone prices excessive can report their concerns to Comcom, which has regulatory tools to intervene in the event of anti-competitive behaviour.

item.title: Bank employees: ASIB accepts UBS regulations
item.description: The ASIB supports the CET-S's proposal to regulate UBS and calls for mandatory social plans as the banking sector faces an unprecedented employment crisis.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ASIB fully supports CET-S proposal to regulate UBS - Calls for mandatory social plans for systemically important institutions - Unemployment in the banking sector has reached the levels of the 2010 crisis - Raiffeisen and Swiss Life announce significant redundancies
## Key Facts - **What**: Federal regulation for the regulation of UBS as a systemic bank - Who: Swiss Association of Bank Employees (ASIB) and Commission for Economic Affairs and Taxation of the States (CET-S) - Where: Switzerland, federal parliamentary debate - When: Proposal in the parliamentary deliberation phase - Main requirements: Mandatory social plans, binding inclusion of employee interests, additional UBS capital - Employment environment: Unemployment at 2010 level, Raiffeisen and Swiss Life redundancies, relocation of Vontobel headquarters
The Swiss Association of Bank Employees (ASIB) has expressed its full support for the proposal of the Commission for Economic Affairs and Taxation of the States (CET-S) for the regulation of UBS as a systemically important bank. In a recently issued statement, the union particularly welcomes the binding inclusion of employees' interests in the future regulation of the sector, a victory strongly advocated by the trade union movement.
### ASIB's claims The union has made a clear demand: the introduction of mandatory social plans for systemically important institutions. According to the ASIB, this measure is crucial at a time when the banking sector is going through an extremely difficult economic situation. The unemployment rate in the sector has already reached the critical levels recorded during the global financial crisis of 2010. In addition, the ASIB draws attention to the recently announced waves of redundancies by Raiffeisen and Swiss Life, as well as the relocation of the Vontobel headquarters. According to the union, these developments show that bank workers are under increasing and unprecedented pressure in the sector.
### The balance of the regulatory proposal The CET-S proposal on additional capital requirements for UBS was welcomed by the ASIB. The union acknowledges that the compromise worked out by the committee adequately balances the need for stability of the Swiss financial hub with the need to preserve the employment levels of bank staff. Natalia Ferrara, vice-president of the ASIB, said in the statement: "The committee's proposal ensures a strong and stable Swiss financial centre and, at the same time, the jobs of bank staff." Parliament was urged to continue with determination along the path outlined by the CET-S and to give its final support to the overall regulatory package. ### Context of crisis in the banking sector The ASIB's support for the CET-S regulation emerges from an analysis of a very serious employment situation in the Swiss financial sector. When the unemployment rate reaches the levels of the 2010 crisis, it means that the bank labor market is under significant structural stresses. The waves of redundancies announced by Raiffeisen and Swiss Life, together with the relocation of the Vontobel headquarters, signal that the large credit institutions are undergoing deep restructuring. In this scenario, the mandatory social plans proposed by the ASIB are not an ancillary demand, but an essential protection for workers who risk losing their jobs. The CET-S proposal recognizes this urgency and codifies it in regulatory form.

item.title: UBS challenges CET-S proposal on capital requirements
item.description: The big bank appreciates the Commission's work but criticizes the new capital requirements, which would cost a total of 30 billion dollars.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - UBS welcomes CET-S but criticizes proposed capital requirements - Proposal would result in $30 billion in additional capital - CEO Ermotti: positive international AT1 alignment, negative costs - Debate will continue in the coming months in Parliament
## Key Facts - **Who**: UBS and the Committee on Economic Affairs Council of States (CET-S) - What: CET-S proposal on capital requirements; UBS appreciates work, criticizes costs - When: Press release issued today; debate next months - Where: Switzerland (financial centre, Federal Parliament) - Amount: ~$30 billion in total additional Tier 1 capital - Proposed regime: 50% CET1 + 50% AT1 for overseas subsidiaries - Source: UBS (press release via Keystone-SDA)
UBS acknowledges the work of the Committee on Economic Affairs and Taxation of the Council of States (CET-S) on the new capital requirements, but has expressed a negative opinion on the concrete proposal. In a statement released today, the large Zurich-based bank argues that the CET-S recommendations would lead to a significant increase in costs for the company.
### The figures of the CET-S proposal
The fee would oblige UBS to build up additional Tier 1 capital of around USD 13 billion, equivalent to around CHF 10 billion, to be covered by AT1 capital. This would be supplemented by an additional USD 2 billion of CET1 capital required by the ordinance amendments announced by the Federal Council. In addition, for the acquisition of Credit Suisse, UBS must maintain additional CET1 capital of around USD 15 billion, in accordance with the applicable rules. Overall, according to UBS's calculation, the institution is expected to build up around USD 30 billion of Tier 1 capital.
However, the changes at the ordinance level should also lead to a relief: at the consolidated group level, a reduction of 4 billion in CET1 capital.
### The proposal compared to the current regime
The CET-S proposes to provide UBS's foreign subsidiaries with 50% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital and 50% with AT1 bonds. After the collapse of Credit Suisse, the Federal Council had suggested full coverage with CET1. The current regime provides for 45% CET1 and 15% AT1.
UBS remains one of the three major institutions in the Swiss financial centre. CEO Sergio Ermotti said via LinkedIn that UBS appreciates the committee's efforts to evaluate alternatives to the Federal Council's extreme proposals. Ermotti also mentioned positively the fact that the CET-S intends to align Swiss AT1 instruments more closely with international practice, thus improving their loss-absorbing capacity at an early stage of the crisis. Both Ermotti and Chairman of the Board Colm Kelleher addressed employees with the same message. ### Implications for the Swiss economy
According to UBS, the CET-S proposal, along with a series of other regulatory measures, would further increase financing costs for the Swiss financial market and the entire Swiss economy. The bank has raised this concern in an international context where other major financial centers are instead simplifying and streamlining their regulatory frameworks for banks.
The increase in financing costs can have indirect effects on the entire national economy: investment projects become more expensive, small and medium-sized enterprises face higher interest rates for financing, and the competitiveness of the Swiss market could suffer compared to other global financial jurisdictions.
### Three scenarios compared
The current regime (45% CET1 + 15% AT1) remains the most lenient for UBS in terms of capital structuring costs. The CET-S proposal (50% CET1 + 50% AT1) represents a compromise between the stricter requirements and the current ones, but it still involves a significant increase in the necessary capital. The original proposal of the Federal Council (100% CET1), advanced after the collapse of Credit Suisse, was the most stringent and would have been even more burdensome for the institution.
The CET-S has chosen to position itself halfway: it recognizes the need to tighten controls post-Credit Suisse, but seeks to do so in a less burdensome way for UBS and for the competitiveness of the market.
### The value of positive recognition
UBS recognizes that the CET-S has taken into account important facts and contexts in formulating its recommendations. This is significant: it means that the dialogue between the bank and the commission is constructive, even where positions diverge. In particular, the recognition of the will to harmonize Swiss AT1 instruments with international practice is positive, as it makes these instruments more effective in containing losses in the initial phase of a banking crisis.
### Global competitive pressures
UBS's communication highlights a broader theme: global competitive pressure. If Switzerland applies significantly higher capital requirements than other global financial jurisdictions, Swiss banks could be at a competitive disadvantage. This could lead to the migration of financial activities to other countries, with consequences for employment in the Swiss financial sector and for federal and cantonal tax revenues. The structuring of financing costs therefore remains a critical issue for the national economy.

There is no formal deadline yet announced in the source, but the Swiss parliamentary process for complex regulatory matters can take several months.
UBS management said it will continue to ensure that the bank contributes constructively to the debate in the months ahead.

The Federal Council remains an important player in this matter. Changes are already announced at the ordinance level (not the law), which means that the federal executive has significant room for movement without necessarily going through parliament. However, the decision to require a capital structuring (50% CET1 + 50% AT1) by the CET-S suggests that parliament wants to have its say on an issue that it considers crucial for the stability of the Swiss banking system after the Credit Suisse crisis.

## In brief - The reference mortgage interest rate remains at 1.25% - The average interest rate is 1.31% - The next update is scheduled for December 1, 2026
## Key Facts - **What**: Reference mortgage rate - When: September 1, 2026 - Where: Switzerland - Who: Federal Office for Housing (FOH) - Amount: 1.25 %
The reference mortgage rate in Switzerland remains at 1.25%, as announced by the Federal Office for Housing (FOH) on 1 September 2026. This rate, which is decisive for determining rents throughout Switzerland, remained unchanged compared to the previous quarter. The average interest rate, calculated as at 30 June 2026, still stands at 1.31%. With commercial rounding, the reference mortgage rate therefore continues to be 1.25% and applies from 2 September 2026. It will remain at this level until the average rate falls below 1.13% or exceeds 1.37%.

Since 2 September 2025, the reference mortgage rate has been 1.25% and has remained unchanged compared to the previous quarter. Therefore, there has been no entitlement to rent increases or decreases since the last publication. In most cases, the lease agreement or the latest rent adjustment notice provides information on the level of the reference interest rate on which the current rent is based. In addition to the change in the reference interest rate, other cost factors, such as changes in the national consumer price index (inflation), may play a role in the calculation of rent. Meanwhile, at the consolidated group level, the ordinance amendments announced in early 2026 are expected to result in a 4 billion reduction in CET1 capital, a partial balancing of the overall charges. ### Why UBS opposes the proposed measures UBS does not deny the importance of financial stability, but argues that the proposed measures go beyond international standards. item.title: Penalties of up to 30 thousand francs for unrest
item.description: Motion by the UDC and the Federal Democratic Union in Mendrisio calls for reimbursement of police and firefighters' expenses for those who cause unrest. Amount up to 30 thousand francs.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Motion by UDC Mendrisio and Federal Democratic Union at City Hall - Penalties of up to 30 thousand francs for those who cause disorder - Reimbursement of police, fire brigade and rescue services costs
## Key Facts - **What**: Proposed reimbursement of expenses for unauthorized use of public property - Where: Mendrisio (Ticino) - Who: Lucio Lorenzon (first signatory) + 6 co-signatories of UDC and Federal Democratic Union - When: Motion presented in these days - Standard amount: 10,000 francs per person - Maximum amount: CHF 30,000 in serious cases - New rule: Article 15 bis of the municipal regulation
Lucio Lorenzon and six other co-signatories of the UDC Mendrisio and the Federal Democratic Union have presented a motion to the City Hall that introduces a simple principle: whoever breaks, pays. The proposal aims to transfer the costs of public disorder from the whole community to those who concretely cause them.
The motion is entitled "Stop passing on the costs to the community: those who cause disorder or demonstrate illegally assume the costs of police interventions" and calls for the introduction of "an obligation to reimburse disturbers in the event of unauthorized use of administrative assets or authorization holders who do not comply with the conditions set by the authority".
The signatories propose to add a new article 15 bis to the municipal regulation. Who will have to pay? Two categories of responsible: people who use public property without authorization or who knowingly violate the rules, and authorization holders who do not comply with the conditions imposed by the administration.
### Refundable expenses and amounts
Eligible costs include police, fire and rescue services, as well as costs caused by the disruption of a public service. The reimbursement remains within 10,000 francs per person in ordinary cases, but reaches 30,000 francs in serious situations (vandalism, damage to infrastructure, intentional violations). If several people are involved in the same incident, the amount can be claimed from each of them regardless of the number of people responsible.
The motion is not an absolute novelty: it recalls similar rules already adopted in other cantons, such as Bern and Lucerne. In addition, there is a pending cantonal parliamentary initiative presented by Alain Bühler together with about twenty Ticino grand councillors, which goes in the same direction. The proposal is based on a change of perspective: it is not the general taxpayers who cover the costs deriving from abusive demonstrations or damage during events, but those who are concretely responsible for them. This mechanism of direct liability introduces a differentiation between three concrete situations.
First scenario: An unauthorized motorcade occupies a street for hours. The police intervene, perhaps even the fire brigade for safety reasons. Estimated total costs: patrols for 5-6 hours, possible administrative report. Under the new rule, the organizer or participants would receive a notification of reimbursement of up to 10,000 francs. If the damage to public property is more serious (writing, fire, injuries), the figure would jump to 30,000.
Second scenario: An event is authorised, but the authorisation holder does not comply with the set conditions (exceeds the agreed time, changes route, welcomes more people than expected). The administration documents the additional costs and sends the reimbursement notice. Here, the responsibility is escalating: it is up to the holder, not to the individual participants.
### How administrative calculation works
The municipal administration will document all expenses: number of patrols and hours of service of the local police, firefighter interventions, use of rescue vehicles and resources, loss of public services (office closure, interruption of functions). The documentation is the basis of the reimbursement notification. The amount remains in the range of 10,000-30,000 francs per person, regardless of the number of people involved.
The precedent of Bern and Lucerne shows that the issue is not marginal. At the cantonal level, the initiative of Bühler and the grand councilors signals that the debate on the distribution of the public costs of the riots is already heated in Ticino as well. Mendrisio could become the first Ticino municipality to legislate on this issue, creating a model that other municipalities could follow.

If the Municipality of Mendrisio approves the motion, the new article 15 bis will come into force according to the ordinary administrative procedure. From that moment, the reimbursement procedure becomes part of the operational management of public disorders.
Anyone who organizes an event must acquire municipal authorization in advance. If the conditions are respected (time, route, maximum number of participants), no refund. If it violates them or if the event is completely abusive, the procedure is triggered.
### The administrative procedure and the right of appeal
The municipal administration calculates the costs incurred and sends a formal notice of reimbursement. The person concerned receives documentation of the services provided (police hours, specific interventions, loss of services). The amount proposed is not arbitrary but based on predefined administrative fees.
An important right arises here: the notice of reimbursement is an administrative measure, not a criminal sanction. The recipient can challenge it with the municipal conciliation authority within the time limits provided for by the ordinance. If the reimbursement is deemed unfair in terms of amount or attribution of liability, the ordinary administrative appeal is always available.

item.title: Novartis suspends clinical trials, +5% on the stock market
item.description: Novartis has stopped studies on rap-cel due to three deaths; at the same time it announces positive results on Remibrutinib. Stock +5% today, +19% YTD.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Novartis discontinues studies on rap-cel, 3 deaths from hemodialysis syndrome - Positive results for Remibrutinib in multiple sclerosis (2,000 patients) - Action gains +5%, +19% year-to-date
## Key Facts - **What**: Suspension of clinical trials of rapcabtagene autoleucel (rap-cel) - When: End of August 2026 - Who: Swiss pharmaceutical giant Novartis - Cause: Three deaths from hemodialysis syndrome - Amount: Stock +5% today, +19% YTD, +27% over 12 months
Novartis halted several clinical trials of experimental cell treatments against autoimmune diseases in the fields of immunology and neuroscience at the end of August. The Swiss company confirmed the news following the deaths of three patients involved in these research programs, ATS told the news agency.
The cause of the suspension is the notification of three cases of hemodialylic syndromes associated with immune effector cells, the complications of which have had fatal outcomes. The experimental treatment, called rapcabtagene autoleucel (or rap-cel), is based on a cell therapy known as CAR-T, which genetically modifies a patient's white blood cells to induce them to destroy defective cells.
Death due to an immune reaction is a known risk for this type of therapeutic approach. US competitor Bristol-Myers-Squibb had previously suspended similar studies as a precautionary measure, confirming that the risks associated with CAR-T therapies fall within the routine management of clinical research.
However, Novartis was keen to emphasize that the program on rap-cel in oncology is absolutely not affected by the suspension, thus maintaining the continuity of studies in the oncology field.
### Concurrently: Positive results on Remibrutinib
On the same day, Novartis announced positive results from two phase III clinical trials, called Remodel-1 and Remodel-2, which evaluated the effectiveness of the active ingredient Remibrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis. The studies involved approximately 2,000 patients worldwide.
Remibrutinib demonstrated a significant reduction in the annual relapse rate compared to the comparator drug Teriflunomide. It is an oral drug that selectively inhibits an enzyme involved in the activation of immune cells. Novartis plans to present the full data at the MStoronto2026 scientific congress in Canada, and then initiate marketing authorization procedures with the global regulatory authorities.
Remibrutinib has already gained approval in the United States and Europe under the trade name Rhapsido for the treatment of chronic spontaneous urticaria, a skin disease characterized by recurrent itching and the appearance of wheals.
### Market reaction
The news was well received on the stock market: Novartis shares gained about 5% in today's session. Since the beginning of the year, the stock has gained 19%, while the performance over longer periods has been largely positive: +27% over twelve months and +63% over five years.
Novartis is one of the twenty largest stocks on the SMI, the index of the most important stocks on the Swiss Stock Exchange. The performance of the stock directly influences the capital gains of those who hold direct shares, which is relevant at the [dichiarazione delle imposte](nav:tax-return) level and for many Swiss investor portfolios. ### Risk management in advanced therapies
CAR-T therapies represent an innovative but complex approach in the treatment of autoimmune and oncological diseases. Hemodialysis syndrome, of which Novartis has reported three fatal cases, is a rare but known complication of these therapies. It is therefore not a completely unexpected event, but rather a risk managed through precautionary withdrawal protocols when the number of adverse events exceeds certain tolerability thresholds.
The fact that Bristol-Myers-Squibb has previously adopted the same suspension strategy indicates that the global pharmaceutical industry is taking these risks into account as part of the regulatory development process. Novartis' decision to maintain studies in oncology, while suspending those in immunology and neuroscience, suggests a differentiated assessment of benefits and risks depending on the target pathology.
### Implications for Swiss investors
For those who own Novartis shares within a Swiss portfolio, or for those who invest through [conti bancari](nav:banks) that include the stock, the latest news reflects a mixed dynamic. The suspension of some studies represents a temporary drag in the pipeline, but the positive results of Remibrutinib offset this loss of momentum. This balance is evident from the stock's 5% rise despite the bad news about the suspension: the market is viewing the announcements overall as net progress thanks to the strength of the Remibrutinib data.
Novartis' position as one of the twenty main values of the SMI means that changes in its stock directly affect the performance of the national index. For Swiss savers with exposure to the local stock market (via ETFs on the SMI, pension funds with a Swiss equity component, or direct investments), this volatility is a daily reality that requires monitoring.
### Swiss pharmaceutical innovation
Novartis remains one of the most important companies for the Swiss economy, not only as a market force but also as an R&D center. The company's ability to manage complex clinical trials, suspend studies when necessary, and advance promising pipelines (such as Remibrutinib) reflects the robustness of the Swiss pharmaceutical industry. The presentation of the data at the MStoronto2026 congress and the subsequent application for authorization from global regulatory authorities underscore how Novartis operates in a global context, but R&D decisions remain strongly rooted in Switzerland.

If you hold Novartis shares or funds that include the stock, it is important to follow future developments on Remibrutinib. The presentation of data at the MStoronto2026 conference will be a critical moment to assess whether the positive results of the Remodel-1 and Remodel-2 studies will continue to find favor with global regulatory authorities. Approvals in the USA and Europe could significantly influence the stock price in the coming months.
Similarly, the resumption of suspended studies on rap-cel will depend on a complete analysis of the safety data. Novartis has stated that it is carefully evaluating the emerging data to determine future steps, suggesting that a reopening could be possible if safety measures are strengthened. Staying informed about these developments allows for informed decisions about your portfolio.

The suspension of studies is not a defeat but a regular step in the drug development cycle. Phase III clinical trials, such as Remodel-1 and Remodel-2, involve thousands of patients and collect data on efficacy and safety. Positive results in this phase authorize companies to proceed with formal regulatory approval requests. In the case of Remibrutinib, the company has already achieved approvals in the USA and Europe for one indication (chronic spontaneous urticaria) and is now seeking to extend use to more serious diseases like multiple sclerosis.

item.title: Mobile telephony, the auction starts at 855 million
item.description: ComCom launches the auction for mobile frequencies with a base of 855 million. Applications by 3 December, assignment in 2027, concessions from 2029 for 15 years.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ComCom announces auction for mobile radio frequencies with a base of CHF 855 million - Applications by 3 December, assignment in 2027, concessions from 1 January 2029 - New concessions valid for 15 years
## Key Facts - **Who**: Federal Communications Commission (ComCom) - What: Auction for the renewal of mobile radio frequencies for Swisscom, Sunrise, Salt - When: Applications until 3 December; Q2 2027 award; concessions from 1 January 2029 - Where: Switzerland (at federal level) - Starting price: CHF 854.7 million - Duration: 15 years
The Federal Communications Commission (ComCom) has announced the launch of the auction for the renewal of mobile radio frequencies in Switzerland. The minimum basis for the tender has been set at CHF 854.7 million. The three largest telephone companies—Swisscom, Sunrise and Salt—can apply by 3 December, with the allocation of frequencies expected in the second quarter of 2027. The new licences will be valid from 1 January 2029 for a period of 15 years.
### Expiring concessions
The frequencies auctioned are identical to those allocated in 2012, which are currently used by Swisscom, Sunrise and Salt. Since these licences expire at the end of December 2028, ComCom must initiate a new allocation procedure. The competent body emphasises that the main objectives are to maintain and develop three high-quality mobile communications networks and to promote competition in the market for the benefit of Swiss consumers.
### Historical comparison: the 2012 auction
In 2012, the last auction for the same frequencies, the minimum bid was set at 637 million francs. The final result was significantly higher: the three telephone companies went as far as a total of 996.3 million francs. Swisscom secured 42% of the available spectrum for a total of 360 million, while Sunrise paid over 500 million despite acquiring fewer frequencies than its dominant rival. Orange (now Salt) paid out 155 million.
### Pricing strategies by frequency bands
ComCom has adopted a strategy of variable prices depending on the frequency range. For low frequencies (800 and 900 megahertz), known for their wide range and good coverage inside buildings, the initial price has been tripled compared to the legal minimum. The mid-range (1800 and 2100 megahertz), which is in great demand by operators because it offers a good compromise between range and speed, has seen the price doubled. For high frequencies (2600 megahertz), the authority has kept the value at the minimum regulatory requirements required by the regulations. ### Protection of competition and limits on supply
In order to curb Swisscom's hegemony, ComCom has reintroduced structural limits on supply. A single operator may not acquire more than 43% of the spectrum subject to limitations. This threshold is designed to ensure that all participants—including established entrants and operators—can have a sufficient allocation to meet their network needs. By 2012, Swisscom had already reached 42%, a concentration against which ComCom intends to put a structural brake in order to protect the competitive momentum of the market.
This protection of competition also serves the interests of small operators and any new entrants wishing to enter the Swiss market, although ComCom acknowledges that entry into the mobile market remains a significant challenge.
### Balance between federal revenues and network quality
Although ComCom must generate appropriate revenue from the sale of these limited resources, the body has made it clear that the purpose of the auction is not to maximize revenues for the Confederation. The balance between two objectives—sustainable federal revenues and maintaining the competitive quality of the networks—remains central to ComCom's assessment.
The competent body admits that it cannot provide a firm estimate of actual revenue, as the result will depend on demand and the behaviour of the participants during the tender. The comparison with 2012 is illuminating: the base of 637 million was exceeded by a total of 359 million, an indication that competition between operators can push prices well beyond the initial threshold. If similar dynamics were to occur in 2027, revenues for the Confederation could rise significantly compared to the basic 854.7 million.
### Technological neutrality and innovation
Licences will be issued on the principle of technology neutrality. Network operators remain free to choose which mobile transmission technologies to use—whether 4G, 5G or other future solutions. This approach allows operators to invest according to their own network strategies without predefined technological constraints, fostering innovation and rapid adaptation to market and consumer needs.

Swiss mobile consumers will be able to feel the effects of this tender mainly on prices and quality of services from 2029, when the new licences come into force. Although the current operators (Swisscom, Sunrise, Salt) remain the main candidates, ComCom has kept open the possibility of new operators participating, while admitting that entry into the mobile market is a significant challenge. Competition between the three main operators, facilitated by the new supply caps (maximum 43% of spectrum per operator), should theoretically contain price margins and push for improvements in services.
Continuity remains guaranteed: the current concessions will remain valid until the end of 2028, so there will be no interruption of service during the transition to the new concessions that will start on January 1, 2029.
### Timeline and key deadlines
The important dates to remember to follow the development of the auction are: - **3 December**: Deadline for submission of applications - Second quarter 2027: Official allocation of frequencies by ComCom - 1 January 2029: Start of validity of new licences - 31 December 2043: End of the concession (15 years from 2029)
To stay up to date with developments, prices and offers from telephone providers, users can regularly consult the official website of ComCom (www.comcom.admin.ch) and follow the announcements of the three main operators.

If you want to optimize your telephone costs, you should regularly consider switching providers or negotiate with your current provider when your contract allows it, especially in view of the possible competitive developments that will follow the 2027 auction. Using provider comparison tools allows you to assess which offers become more competitive over time. The technological neutrality guaranteed by ComCom means that consumers can expect innovations and improvements in the quality of 4G and 5G services offered by the operators that win the auction.

item.title: Companies detect skills shortages in apprentices
item.description: Survey by Economiesuisse reveals critical gaps in writing and mathematics among Swiss apprentices. Three-quarters of companies provide additional support.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Critical writing and math skills among Swiss apprentices - Continuous worsening over the last 5-10 years according to the survey - 75% of companies provide additional support to fill gaps
## Key Facts - **What**: Survey on deficiencies in apprentices' basic skills - When: Published today by Economiesuisse, USAM and USI - Where: Swiss companies from various sectors - Who: Economiesuisse, USAM (Union of Arts and Crafts), USI (Union of Entrepreneurs) - Sample: Approximately 2,900 training managers surveyed - Trend: Continuous deterioration over the last 5-10 years - Support: ~75% of companies provide additional support measures
Economiesuisse, the Swiss Association of Arts and Crafts (SAM) and the Swiss Employers' Association (USI) today published a survey that provides a snapshot of a structural problem in Swiss vocational and professional education: most companies are experiencing significant gaps in the basic skills of their apprentices.
The survey, which surveyed around 2,900 training managers from different companies, reveals that the deterioration is continuous. Over the past five to ten years, the shortages have worsened significantly. Writing skills and mathematical skills – two skills that are fundamental for the success of vocational training – suffer the most.
### The survey data
The consequences for companies are not theoretical. It is becoming more difficult to recruit suitable apprentices, the burden of care is increasing, and additional support measures are costing organisations considerably. To address the problem, around three-quarters of companies – 75% to be precise – already support apprentices with additional internal or external measures in order to close existing gaps.
This means that companies are investing significant resources to compensate for the shortcomings found when entering the training course. A financial and organizational burden that falls directly on company budgets and their ability to manage the Swiss dual vocational education and training system, one of the pillars of the national economy.
The study represents the convergent opinion of three key players in the Swiss business world: Economiesuisse, which represents the interests of companies at the national level; the USAM, which protects arts and crafts; and USI, the entrepreneurs' union. Their joint voice underlines the urgency of addressing the issue in a structural way. ### The context of the worsening
The negative trend in the survey is not episodic. The continuous deterioration over the past five to ten years reflects broader changes in the Swiss education system. Basic skills – in particular writing and numeracy – are the foundation on which dual vocational education and training, a system that traditionally enjoys a high international reputation, is based.
When these fundamental skills are scarce, the entire training process suffers. Apprentices struggle to follow specialized technical teaching, trainers devote hours to remedial lessons that should have been addressed during compulsory schooling, and companies find themselves managing unexpected organizational complexity.
### The concrete economic consequences
The fact that three-quarters of companies already provide additional support measures is not a solution – it is a symptom of a structural problem. It means that the system is "absorbing" the deficit, but at the expense of profitability and business efficiency.
Internal and external measures come at a cost: dedicated trainer hours, specialised external courses, additional personalised mentoring. The study clearly points out that the costs are considerable – although not quantified in precise figures – and are borne by the organisations that manage apprenticeships.
In addition to the financial impact, the difficulty in recruiting suitable apprentices puts the very continuity of the dual education system at risk. If companies cannot find candidates with the necessary basic skills, the qualification cycle is interrupted. Fewer quality apprentices mean fewer qualified professionals in the Swiss labour market, which has consequences for national competitiveness in the long term.
The three associations – Economiesuisse, USAM and USI – represent hundreds of thousands of jobs in Switzerland and directly manage vocational education and training. Their joint alarm is not speculative, but the direct response of those who experience this problem on a daily basis: gaps in basic skills have become a concrete and measurable obstacle.

The fact that 75% of companies provide additional support indicates that the private sector is not waiting for an institutional solution, but is acting autonomously. These measures include both internal and external interventions: personalized tutoring programs, Italian and mathematics lessons taught by specialized company trainers, use of external training institutions for recovery, or partnerships with recognized school support centers.
However, not all companies have the resources to bear these additional costs. Larger companies can afford dedicated training and recovery teams; small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) – the backbone of the Swiss economy – are in a more fragile position. Investing an additional budget to fill gaps that should be addressed in compulsory education generates pressure on profit margins and reduces the ability to invest in technological innovation and infrastructure.
### The role of vocational education and training in the Swiss labour market
Swiss dual vocational education and training remains one of the most popular and efficient systems in the world. However, the survey shows that the system is starting to show cracks in its foundations. If basic skills are not adequately transmitted in compulsory schooling, the task falls on those who manage the further training: companies and vocational centres.
The approximately 2,900 education managers interviewed in the survey come from different sectors of the Swiss economy. Their converging testimony is a wake-up call that deserves attention from federal and cantonal institutions. The cantons manage compulsory education and will have to coordinate with employers' associations and the Federal Administration to reverse the trend in the coming years.
In the meantime, those who intend to undertake an apprenticeship should be aware that basic skills in writing and numeracy are not optional: they are the prerequisites for not falling behind classmates and for seizing the best training opportunities. Investing in strengthening these skills before enrolling in a career path represents a concrete competitive advantage in the Swiss labor market. Many cantons and municipalities offer free summer remedial courses; the career guidance center in your canton is the first point of contact for identifying available resources.
